prompt: `network.sh` ran once and created a VPC, a subnet and a security group. Which question can the script itself answer a month later?
hint: A script records what was done on the day it ran.

choices.text: What exists in the account today
choices.why: Only AWS knows that; the script never looks.

choices.text: Which commands were sent the day it ran
choices.why: Yes. That is all a list of steps records: what was asked for, once.

choices.text: What a colleague changed by hand since then
choices.why: A change made elsewhere leaves no trace in the file.

choices.text: What a second run of it would do
choices.why: Nothing in it says; the lesson had to run it to find out, and got a second VPC.

prompt: Why does `network.sh` capture the output of `create-vpc` into `VPC` instead of just printing it?
hint: Look at what the next two commands need.

choices.text: To print it at the end, for the record
choices.why: It is printed at the end, but that is not why it is kept: the next commands need it.

choices.text: Because AWS refuses a second VPC unless the first id is passed back
choices.why: AWS needs no such thing; the lesson's second run created a second VPC without it.

choices.text: The commands after it need that id
choices.why: Right. The subnet and the security group must name their VPC, and only AWS knows its id.

choices.text: To make the script idempotent
choices.why: Keeping an id does not stop the script creating everything again on the next run.

prompt: A server or network that exists only as the result of a sequence of manual steps, slightly different from every other and impossible to rebuild exactly, is called a ___.
hint: A thing of which no two are alike.

prompt: A colleague opened port 22 on the `web` security group from another machine. What is the gap between that group and `network.sh` called?
hint: It is the name of the lesson's second section.

choices.text: A conflict
choices.why: Nothing conflicted: AWS accepted the change and the file never knew.

choices.text: Drift
choices.why: Yes: what exists has moved away from what was described.

choices.text: A rollback
choices.why: A rollback undoes a change; here a change was added.

choices.text: A replacement of the security group
choices.why: The group kept its id; a rule was added to it in place.

prompt: The team agrees that whoever changes the network by hand will also update `network.sh` afterwards. What does the lesson say about this arrangement?
hint: Who produced the drift in the first place?

choices.text: It is the same arrangement that produced the drift
choices.why: Right. It depends on everybody remembering every time, which is what failed. The cure is making the file the only way a change happens.

choices.text: It cures drift as long as the update happens on the same day
choices.why: The day does not matter; the change still happened before anybody could review it, and nothing checks that the file was updated.

choices.text: It works if the script is kept in version control
choices.why: Version control records edits to the file; it cannot see a change made in the cloud.

choices.text: It makes the change reviewable before it happens
choices.why: The edit to the file comes after the change, so nobody reviews anything in time.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for drift being worse than a missing note? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three reasons, each in bold.

choices.text: It stays invisible until somebody compares
choices.why: Yes; the network works, so nothing prompts anybody to look.

choices.text: It slows the cloud down
choices.why: Drift is a difference in configuration, not in performance.

choices.text: Later changes are built on top of it
choices.why: Yes; it compounds.

choices.text: Nobody could review the change before it happened
choices.why: Yes; it was typed straight into the cloud.

choices.text: AWS deletes resources that drift
choices.why: AWS keeps whatever it is told; it has no idea what was intended.

prompt: Which of these is configuration management rather than provisioning?
hint: Can the cloud's API see it?

choices.text: Creating a subnet in `sa-east-1a`
choices.why: A subnet is a resource the provider sells: provisioning.

choices.text: Opening port 443 on a security group
choices.why: A security group rule is created through the cloud's API: provisioning.

choices.text: Writing `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` on a running machine
choices.why: Yes. A file inside the operating system is invisible to the cloud's API.

choices.text: Creating a bucket for the shop's images
choices.why: A bucket is a provider resource: provisioning.

prompt: Match each tool to the job the lesson gives it.
hint: Three jobs, one of them about images.

prompt: Ana could create the shop's VPC with Ansible's cloud modules. Why does the lesson call that the second-best tool for the job?
hint: Think about what happens when a line is deleted.

choices.text: Ansible cannot talk to the AWS API at all
choices.why: It can; the lesson says it works. The problem is what it remembers.

choices.text: It keeps no record of what it created
choices.why: Right. Without a record, deleting a line removes nothing: it cannot tell which resources are its own.

choices.text: Ansible needs an agent installed in the VPC
choices.why: A VPC has no operating system to install anything in, and Ansible pushes over SSH anyway.

choices.text: YAML cannot describe a network range
choices.why: A range is a string; any format can carry it.

prompt: Terraform starts a machine and runs a script on it once, at creation, that installs nginx. Six months later somebody edits nginx's file on that machine by hand. What does the next `terraform apply` do about it?
hint: Which layer is the edited file in?

choices.text: Runs the creation script again and restores the file
choices.why: A script run at creation is never run again; that is the lesson's point about it.

choices.text: Replaces the machine, because its configuration changed
choices.why: Terraform cannot see a file inside the machine, so it sees no change.

choices.text: Nothing: the file is inside the OS, where the cloud's API cannot look
choices.why: Right. The machine's attributes match, so Terraform reports no changes, and the edit drifts on.

choices.text: Reports the edited file as drift
choices.why: That would need it to read the disk, which is configuration management's job.

prompt: What did running `network.sh` a second time produce?
hint: Look at the `describe-vpcs` that followed.

choices.text: An error, because a VPC named `shop` already existed
choices.why: AWS does not treat the Name tag as unique; it accepted the second one.

choices.text: Nothing, because the VPC was already there
choices.why: That is what `terraform apply` did; the script never checks.

choices.text: A second VPC with the same name and range
choices.why: Yes: two VPCs called `shop`, both `10.20.0.0/16`.

choices.text: A new subnet inside the existing VPC
choices.why: The script creates a new VPC first and puts the subnet in that one.

prompt: An operation that leaves the world the same whether it runs once or twice is called ___.
hint: The property `terraform apply` has and `network.sh` lacks.

prompt: The second `terraform apply` printed `No changes.` What did Terraform do before deciding that?
hint: Read the first line of that output.

choices.text: Read the existing VPC back from AWS and compared it with the file
choices.why: Yes: `Refreshing state...` is the read, and the comparison found nothing to do.

choices.text: Checked the file's modification time
choices.why: Terraform compares content with the real resource, not timestamps.

choices.text: Created the VPC again and deleted the duplicate
choices.why: It created nothing: `0 added`.

choices.text: Asked AWS whether any VPC called `shop-tf` was in use
choices.why: It looked up its own VPC by the id it remembered, not by name.

prompt: To compare, Terraform has to know which real VPC belongs to which line of the file. Where does that knowledge live?
hint: Lessons 7 and 8 are about it.

choices.text: In the Name tag
choices.why: Tags can be changed by anybody, and two VPCs shared one in this very lesson.

choices.text: In the state, Terraform's record of what it made
choices.why: Yes; the script needed none because it never asked anything.

choices.text: In AWS, which remembers which tool created each resource
choices.why: AWS keeps no such link; the second VPC from the script looks exactly like the first.

choices.text: In `main.tf`, after the first apply writes the id into it
choices.why: Terraform never edits your configuration; the file shown is the one ana wrote.

prompt: After `network.sh` ran twice and `terraform apply` ran twice, how many VPCs had Ana created in total?
hint: Two from one, one from the other.

prompt: Under immutable infrastructure, how does a new version of the web server reach production?
hint: Nothing running is edited.

choices.text: A tool logs in to each machine and upgrades the package
choices.why: That is the mutable column: editing what runs.

choices.text: New machines replace the old ones
choices.why: Yes: new machines are built with it, put in service, and the old ones destroyed.

choices.text: The machines are rebooted so they pick up the new version
choices.why: A reboot runs what is already on the disk; something still has to put the new version there.

choices.text: It is copied into place and the service restarted
choices.why: Copying into a running machine is an in-place change.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep a database on the mutable side even in a shop that replaces everything else?
hint: What would be thrown away with it?

choices.text: Databases cannot be created by Terraform
choices.why: They can; the question is whether to throw one away for each change.

choices.text: Its value is the data that has built up on it
choices.why: Right. Replacing it would replace the data, so the state is kept in a few managed places.

choices.text: Database servers are pets by law
choices.why: No law says so; it is a design decision.

choices.text: Immutable machines are slower to start
choices.why: Start-up time is not the reason given; the data is.

prompt: Match each situation to what the lesson's table says happens.
hint: Two columns, two rows of the table.

pairs.right: An edit to what is running
A new copy, then a swap
Undo the edit, if anybody knows what it was

prompt: Which tool in the lesson's table provisions only AWS, from YAML or JSON templates?
hint: It is AWS's own.

choices.text: Pulumi
choices.why: Pulumi works with any provider, in general-purpose languages.

choices.text: OpenTofu
choices.why: OpenTofu is the Terraform fork, written in HCL for any provider.

choices.text: CloudFormation
choices.why: Yes; the AWS CDK generates its templates from code.

choices.text: Salt
choices.why: Salt is configuration management.

prompt: In Terraform, what is a provider?
hint: Terraform itself knows nothing about AWS.

choices.text: The cloud company that bills the account
choices.why: In everyday speech, yes; in Terraform the word names a program.

choices.text: A program that knows one API
choices.why: Yes. It turns resource blocks into that API's calls and reads the result back; there is one per API.

choices.text: The `provider` block's region setting
choices.why: The block configures the provider; the region is one of its arguments.

choices.text: A module published on the registry
choices.why: Modules are lesson 10 and are written in HCL; providers are compiled programs.

prompt: A team wants one tool that both creates its cloud network and keeps nginx's files right on thirty running machines. What does the lesson recommend instead?
hint: The table has no row for it.

choices.text: Terraform for both, with a creation script for nginx
choices.why: A creation script runs once and then drifts.

choices.text: Ansible for both, since it has cloud modules
choices.why: It keeps no record of what it created.

choices.text: Two tools, with a clear line between them
choices.why: Yes: one for provisioning, one for configuration or Packer. Lesson 18 draws that line between Terraform and Ansible.

choices.text: CloudFormation, which covers everything on AWS
choices.why: It is a provisioning tool; it does not manage files inside machines either.

prompt: In the lab, what makes the AWS CLI and Terraform talk to moto instead of to Amazon?
hint: One of the four variables.

choices.text: `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=sa-east-1`
choices.why: That chooses the region, wherever the endpoint is.

choices.text: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test`
choices.why: A key says who is asking, not where the request goes.

choices.text: `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566`
choices.why: Yes: every call goes to that address.

choices.text: `provider "aws" { region = "sa-east-1" }`
choices.why: The provider block is the same as for a real account; that is the point.

prompt: moto accepted `aws_instance` and returned an id. What does that instance actually do in the lab?
hint: moto imitates the API, not the machines behind it.

choices.text: It runs on the laptop as a small virtual machine
choices.why: moto runs nothing; lessons 18 to 20 use containers when a running machine is needed.

choices.text: It answers on port 443 like a real server
choices.why: No packet reaches it; there is nothing to answer.

choices.text: Nothing: it is a record with an id and a state
choices.why: Right, and that is exactly what Terraform reads back.

choices.text: It is created in a real AWS account in the background
choices.why: No real account is involved, and nothing is billed.

prompt: At home, `aws sts get-caller-identity` answers `Could not connect to the endpoint URL`. What does the lesson tell you to check first?
hint: Nothing answered at the address.

choices.text: That `moto_server` is running and the port matches `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`
choices.why: Yes; the message means nothing is listening there.

choices.text: That the key pair is `test`
choices.why: A wrong key gives a credentials error, after connecting.

choices.text: That the provider block has the right region
choices.why: The CLI call involves no provider block, and the region does not stop a connection.

choices.text: That Terraform is version 1.16
choices.why: Terraform is not involved in an AWS CLI call.

prompt: Put the steps to follow these lessons on your own computer in order.
hint: moto has to be running before anything asks it something.
items: Install moto and the AWS CLI with pip
Export the four `AWS_` variables in your working terminal
trap: Exporting the variables in moto's own terminal is the usual slip: the terminal you type commands in is the one that needs them.

prompt: A colleague rebuilds the shop's network in a new region by running `network.sh`. SSH works in the old region and not in the new one. Why?
hint: Which rule is in the file, and which only in the old group?

choices.text: Port 22 was opened by hand and never written down
choices.why: Right: the rebuild produced exactly what was written, which is the network without the drift.

choices.text: Security groups cannot be copied from one AWS region to another
choices.why: Nothing was copied; the script created a new group from its own lines.

choices.text: The new VPC has a different range
choices.why: The script uses the same `10.20.0.0/16` everywhere.

choices.text: SSH is blocked in some AWS regions
choices.why: No region blocks it; the group simply has no rule for it.

prompt: Which of these is idempotent?
hint: Running it twice leaves the world as running it once.

choices.text: `aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/16`
choices.why: Each run creates another VPC.

choices.text: `terraform apply` with an unchanged `main.tf`
choices.why: Yes: the second run found no changes.

choices.text: `aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress` for a new rule
choices.why: The second call fails or adds again; either way it is not a description of an end state.

choices.text: `sh network.sh`
choices.why: Its second run made a second network.

prompt: Which statements about the lab are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: moto, the providers, and the bill.

choices.text: The providers are the ones HashiCorp publishes
choices.why: Yes; `terraform init` downloads them from the Terraform Registry, as it would for any configuration.

choices.text: moto keeps what it is told after it stops
choices.why: It keeps everything in memory and forgets it when it stops.

choices.text: Nothing an `apply` makes in moto is billed
choices.why: Yes; moto is a program on your own computer, and there is no account behind it to bill.

choices.text: Terraform prints different plans against moto than against AWS for the same file
choices.why: The plan is computed from the file and the state; moto only answers the API calls.

prompt: Why is `iac-env.sh` read with `. ~/iac-env.sh` rather than run with `sh ~/iac-env.sh`?
hint: Where do the variables a script sets live?

choices.text: A run script sets variables in its own shell
choices.why: Yes. `.` reads the file into the shell you are typing in, so the variables stay.

choices.text: `sh` refuses a file that has no `#!/bin/sh` line at the top
choices.why: `sh file` runs it whatever its first line says; the first line matters to `./file`.

choices.text: `.` runs the file with `sudo`, which the variables need to be set
choices.why: Nothing in the file needs root; `.` runs it as you, in your own shell.

choices.text: Running it with `sh` would start a second copy of moto
choices.why: The file never starts moto; moto runs in a terminal of its own.

prompt: In a new terminal, `aws sts get-caller-identity` answers `Unable to locate credentials`. What is missing?
hint: The CLI was found, so the Python environment is active.

choices.text: The `AWS_` variables: only the venv is active
choices.why: Yes. `. ~/iac-env.sh` sets the key and the endpoint as well as activating the Python environment (the venv).

choices.text: moto: nothing is listening on port 4566 of this computer
choices.why: Then the CLI would say it could not connect to the endpoint URL.

choices.text: The AWS CLI itself, which the setup script never installed
choices.why: Then the shell would say `aws: command not found`.

choices.text: An AWS account, because moto only accepts real keys
choices.why: moto accepts the word `test` as a key; no account exists anywhere in this lab.

prompt: A lesson's first plan finds two VPCs named `shop` where the page shows one. What do you do?
hint: Each lesson was recorded on an empty moto.

choices.text: Restart moto, run `fresh-lesson.sh`, start again
choices.why: Yes. The second VPC is left over from an earlier lesson, and an empty moto is what the page was recorded on.

choices.text: Add the VPC's id to the data source so it matches only one
choices.why: That hides the leftover and ties the file to an id that changes on every run.

choices.text: Delete the default VPC, which is the extra one here
choices.why: The default VPC is not named `shop`; the extra one was made by an earlier lesson.

choices.text: Run `terraform destroy` in the lesson's own directory
choices.why: That directory's state does not know the leftover VPC, so destroy would not touch it.
